title: Finite-momentum trimers and Cooper quartets in a one-dimensional Fermi gas with coexistent $s$- and $p$-wave interactions
abstract: We study finite-momentum trimers and Cooper quartets in a one-dimensional two-component Fermi gas with coexistent $s$- and $p$-wave interactions, regularized in the relative momentum of each pair so that they remain Galilean invariant. Pauli blocking alone then makes the trimer dispersion deviate from free center-of-mass motion, so the trimer energy can be lowest at finite total momentum. Allowing this motion expands the $abb$ region among pairs and trimers and removes the region where an odd-wave pair is lowest. The $aabb$ quartet lies below all these branches at every sampled coupling, and in a strip starting on the crossing of the two dimer-pair channels its lowest breakup channel is a moving $abb$ trimer and an atom. At weak interspecies attraction, a variational bound shows that two odd-wave Cooper pairs bind into a quartet, whose binding exceeds that of the coexisting trimer by orders of magnitude as the attraction weakens. At stronger interspecies attraction, the quartet binding relative to two unlike-species dimers disappears when the odd-wave interaction is switched off, although the even-wave interaction dominates the interaction energy. Relative to the in-vacuum case, the Fermi sea enhances the weak-coupling quartet binding, and at fixed scattering lengths the quartet binding grows with density while the coexisting trimer becomes much shallower. These results show that neither the most strongly bound pair nor the dominant interaction energy alone determines whether the quartet binds.
summary: This paper theoretically examines the formation and binding of Cooper quartets and trimers in a 1D Fermi gas subjected to both s-wave and p-wave interactions. Using variational methods, the authors demonstrate that the quartet binding can be robustly strong, even when considering the competition from other bound states. The findings highlight that the binding mechanism is complex, depending on more than just the strongest pairwise interaction.
main_problem: The study investigates the competition and coexistence of different pairing channels (s-wave and p-wave) and the formation of multi-particle clusters (trimers and Cooper quartets) in a Fermi gas.
main_result: The analysis shows that the Cooper quartet binding can be significantly stronger than the trimer binding, and that the binding is not determined solely by the strongest pair interaction or the dominant interaction energy.
method: The research employs a variational approach to minimize the energy of the multi-particle clusters (trimers and quartets) within the framework of a generalized Cooper theory.
model_or_system: The system is a one-dimensional two-component Fermi gas described by a Hamiltonian including kinetic energy and coexistent s-wave and p-wave attraction terms. Interactions are regularized in the relative momentum to maintain Galilean invariance.
key_observables: Binding energy of the quartet relative to its breakup channels, trimer dispersion, and density dependence of binding.
important_parameters: Coexistence of s- and p-wave interactions, finite total momentum of clusters, and varying interspecies attraction strength.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes equal densities ($k_{F,a} = k_{F,b}$) and is performed above an inert Fermi sea; the variational energy provides an upper bound on the true energy.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate weak-coupling binding scales for the quartet versus the trimer, and show the momentum dependence of trimer and trimer-atom energies at various coupling strengths.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the model Hamiltonian and using variational methods to calculate cluster energies, analyzing the hierarchy of binding energies, and finally comparing in-vacuum versus in-medium (finite density) results.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses complex many-body physics in ultracold atomic gases, specifically the interplay between different pairing symmetries (s-wave vs. p-wave) and the formation of exotic few-body states like quartets.
